attacks.claim: The up migration adds an empty `private_notes` column and drops `notes` without copying data, permanently destroying all users' free-text notes on an automatic deploy. The PR's 'pure rename, no data change' is false. The down migration only re-adds an empty `notes` column, so it cannot restore anything, and no backup or checkpoint precedes the DROP.
attacks.evidence:
ALTER TABLE user_recipes ADD COLUMN private_notes text;
ALTER TABLE user_recipes DROP COLUMN notes; / "Pure rename, no data change; the down migration restores the old name." / ABSENT: any UPDATE copying notes, RENAME COLUMN, or backup step

attacks.claim: The handler removed LIMIT and any keyset predicate. It loads every saved row (200k+ for heavy users, including notes text) on each page request and paginates in JS with findIndex/slice. Per-request work is O(N), a full scroll is quadratic, and the 300ms p99 budget is very likely breached with memory pressure on the API process. No index or query plan is provided.

The migration drops `notes` in the same change that switches code to `private_notes`, and migrations run automatically on deploy. Old pods still selecting `ur.notes` will 500 during the rolling deploy. There is no expand/contract sequencing.
attacks.evidence: Old query: "ur.saved_at, ur.notes"; migration "DROP COLUMN notes"; ABSENT: expand/contract or two-step deploy plan

attacks.claim: ALTER TABLE on a ~140M-row hot table takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock with no lock_timeout, run automatically on deploy. If it queues behind long-running reads, it blocks all traffic on user_recipes.

A stale or unknown cursor (e.g. the recipe was unsaved between pages) makes findIndex return -1, so start becomes 0 and the response silently restarts from page 1. This reproduces the duplicate and loop problem the PR claims to fix.
attacks.evidence: const start = cursor ? rows.findIndex((r) => r.id === cursor) + 1 : 0;

attacks.claim: limit is not clamped to a positive minimum. A negative limit yields an empty page, and `page[page.length - 1].id` can then throw, returning a 500.

The response field is renamed from `notes` to `private_notes` with no shim and no client changes in the diff. Clients reading `notes` will silently show blank notes. The claim that the client already sends `nextCursor` cursors is unsupported, since the old endpoint returned no `nextCursor`.
attacks.evidence: SELECT ... ur.private_notes ... res.json({ items: page, nextCursor }); ABSENT: any client change; old: res.json({ items: rows });

attacks.claim: Offset support is removed silently. Old clients sending `offset` get page 1 every time instead of an error or deprecation path.
attacks.evidence: const cursor = typeof req.query.cursor === "string" ? req.query.cursor : null; (offset no longer read)

attacks.claim: The schema change and API pagination change are bundled, so a problem in either forces rollback of both. Tests cover only a 5-row happy path, with no stale-cursor, limit-edge, or large-dataset cases.
attacks.evidence: "Two small changes bundled because they touch the same table."; test only covers valid cursors on r1–r5
